title: Towards Visual Query Segmentation in the Wild
claim: Prior localization finds only the last occurrence with a coarse box; ours segments every occurrence at the pixel level.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right video filmstrips, query thumbnail at left, timestamps under arrows
description: Two stacked panels, (a) and (b), each shown as horizontal filmstrips of video frames. At the far left of every row is a small query image with a colored outline: a yellow box in (a), yellow masks in (b). Panel (a) shows an office video. A blue box labeled 'ignored' covers the middle frames, where the target is marked 'not labeled'. Only the final frames get a green bounding box, labeled 'last object occurrence' with timestamps 62.6 s to 64.7 s. Panel (b) has two rows, a basketball court and chickens in a yard. Pink pixel-level masks mark the target across several separate segments. Each segment has a double-headed arrow labeled 'object occurrence' with start and end times. Captions beneath each panel state the contrast, with italics on the key phrases.
caption: Comparison of existing VQL paradigm in image (a) and the proposed VQS in image (b).
abstract: In this paper, we introduce visual query segmentation (VQS), a new paradigm of visual query localization (VQL) that aims to segment all pixel-level occurrences of an object of interest in an untrimmed video, given a visual query. Compared with existing VQL locating only the last appearance of a target using bounding boxes, VQS enables more comprehensive (i.e., all object occurrences) and precise (i.e., pixel-level masks) localization, making it more practical for real-world scenarios. To foster research on this task, we introduce VQS-4K, a large-scale benchmark dedicated to VQS. Specifically, VQS-4K consists of 4,111 videos with more than 1.3 million frames, and covers a diverse set of 222 object categories. Each video is paired with a visual query defined by a frame outside search video and its target mask, and annotated with spatial-temporal masklets corresponding to the queried target. To ensure high quality, all videos in VQS-4K are manually labeled with meticulous inspection and iterative refinement. To our best knowledge, VQS-4K is the first benchmark specifically designed for VQS. Furthermore, to stimulate future research, we present a simple yet effective method, named VQ-SAM, which extends SAM 2 by leveraging target-specific and background distractor cues from the video to progressively evolve the memory through a novel multi-stage framework with an adaptive memory generation (AMG) module for VQS, significantly improving the performance. In our experiments on VQS-4K, VQ-SAM achieves promising results and surpasses existing methods, evidencing its effectiveness. With VQS-4K and VQ-SAM, we expect to inspire more future research and applications on VQS. Our benchmark and code are released at https://github.com/VAIL-Fan/VQS.
